entries.why: The Act's scope is prose, not a table. Auto-rewriting which situations are protected from a scraped page would let the site's most consequential sentences change without a person reading them.
The shard is a transcription of statutory text. A statute changes by amendment, rarely and deliberately, and the change must be read rather than parsed.
Eleven clocks across four titles of the CFR, each cited to its own section. A missed enrollment window costs a household its coverage, so a human reads every change.
Channel availability and eligibility change by program announcement, not on a schedule — and an absence (Direct File in 2026) is itself a recorded fact.
The ordering framing and consequence language come from the CFPB's own tool. A change there is a reason to re-read the ordering, not to rewrite it automatically.
The qualifying events that open a special enrollment period. The sequence ordering is editorial; this watches the list it is grounded in.

Delaware's standard deduction is statutory and does not index: 30 Del. C. §1108 has set it at $3,250 / $6,500 for every taxable period beginning after December 31, 1999. There is no annual figure to parse, and the section states the amounts as a history of periods without ever using a filing-status label a parser knows — it says "resident spouses ... if they file a joint return". A value adapter is the wrong instrument; a change here is an amendment, and an amendment must be read.

This shard's consequential content is not its threshold — 138% has been the effective ACA figure since 2014 — but the MAP: which of the 51 jurisdictions expanded, since NFIB v. Sebelius made it optional and a state can change position by ballot measure or legislation. The adapter watches the threshold and refuses, so the map was watched by nothing at all, behind a citation note promising a refresh watch covered it. This is the only Medicaid.gov page that states the map in readable text, one row per state with an 'Expansion to Adults' column reading a percentage or 'No' — but it is dated ('based on state decisions as of December 1, 2023'), so parsing it would confirm a 2026 shard forever and could never report a change, the Rev. Proc. 2023-34 trap. Fingerprinting it is the honest half: CMS republishing the table is what a state changing position looks like here, and a person reads the diff. The map was verified row by row against this page on 2026-08-30 and agrees for all 51.

The $25,000 / $32,000 provisional-income thresholds are statutory and were deliberately never indexed — they have not moved since 1983 and 1993, which is why an ever-growing share of benefits is taxable. There is no annual figure for an adapter to chase, so this is Delaware's shape: a change is an amendment somebody reads. Watched at the statute rather than at Pub 915, which is reissued annually at a stable URL and would fire every year about a rule that had not moved.

The AOTC and Lifetime Learning phase-out ranges do not index: § 25A(i) fixed them at $80,000-$90,000 single and $160,000-$180,000 joint, and the 2020 Act aligned the Lifetime Learning range to the same figures rather than continuing to adjust it. The inflation-adjustment procedure states neither, so there is nothing annual to parse and a change is an act of Congress. This list first recorded the opposite, that the ranges index; the statute is watched now partly so that claim stops being taken on trust.

The Uniform Lifetime Table is a regulation, not an indexed figure. Treasury last reissued it effective 2022, on revised mortality assumptions, and it moves only when they are revised again — a rulemaking, which is exactly the kind of change that must be read rather than parsed. Watched at the regulation that contains the table rather than at Pub 590-B, which restates it and is reissued every year.

The full-retirement-age schedule is statutory (42 U.S.C. 416(l)) and keyed to year of birth, so it does not index and has not moved since the 1983 amendments — Delaware's shape again, where a change is an amendment somebody reads. The figures that DO move annually, the wage base and the COLA, live in fica-2024 and the SSA adapter watches those; this shard holds only the part that does not move, which is exactly why nothing was watching it.

The SALT limitation is statutory, not indexed, and it is on a written schedule: IRC §164(b)(7)(A) sets $40,000 for 2025 and $40,400 for 2026, then 101 percent of the prior year through 2029, then back to $10,000. So there is no annual figure for an adapter to chase and every step is a transcription somebody makes deliberately — Delaware's shape, at the statute rather than at a revenue procedure. It is watched at all because the last version of this figure was a constant in the engine with nothing behind it, which is how it stayed at $10,000 for two years after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act replaced it, understating the deduction for anyone itemizing more than $10,000 of state and local tax.

The applicable-percentage table is reissued each year in its own revenue procedure at a URL nothing predicts, so there is no listing page to watch and the annual indexing stays a reviewer's transcription. What this watches instead is the RULE, which is where the harm lives: §36B(c)(1)(A) is the 100%-to-400% eligibility band, and §36B(c)(1)(B) — the ARPA/IRA suspension of the 400% cliff — was repealed by Pub. L. 119-21 §71302(a) on 2025-07-04, which is why the cliff is back for plan year 2026 and why a household one dollar over 400% of the poverty line loses every dollar of subsidy. A change of that kind makes the shard wrong in kind rather than slightly stale, and it is exactly the change a person must read. Same shape as the §86 and Delaware watches: at the statute, because the annual document is a closed one.

The SAI tables are reissued each award year in the ED SAI Formula Guide, a PDF at a new path, and the Knowledge Center pages that would list it render client-side and return less visible text than the watch's own interstitial floor — so there is nothing there for a fingerprint to hold, and the annual tables stay a reviewer's transcription. This watches the formula instead: HEA §475, 20 U.S.C. §1087oo, which defines the student aid index and its allowances against income — the payroll-tax allowance, the income protection allowance, the employment expense allowance. An amendment there changes what the estimate MEANS, not just its numbers, and this shard's own note already warns the reader to check against the official guide.

IRC §163(h)(4), the deduction for qualified passenger vehicle loan interest, is statutory and unindexed like the SALT limitation beside it: $10,000, reduced by $200 for each $1,000 (or portion thereof) of modified AGI over $100,000 or $200,000 joint, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 and before January 1, 2029. There is no annual figure for an adapter to chase and the section carries its own sunset, so what a person needs to be told is that the text moved — including the day it expires and the shard should stop carrying the rule at all. Second watch on this shard, at a different statute from §164.

§63(b) is the list, and the list is load-bearing twice over. It names what a filer who does not itemize subtracts from adjusted gross income — paragraphs (4) through (7) are §170(p), §224, §225 and §163(h)(4), the four of the Act's five new deductions that reach a non-itemizer — and because it defines federal TAXABLE income it is also the list that six states inherit by starting there. A new paragraph in §63(b) is therefore a change to Colorado, Idaho, Iowa, Montana, North Dakota and Oregon that none of those states legislated, and nothing else in this repo would see it. Third watch on this shard: §164 for the cap, §163 for the car loan, §63 for the list itself.

The Department's own guide is where Colorado states both halves of the conformity answer this shard encodes: that "Colorado income tax is based generally on federal taxable income", and which federal deductions must be added back — overtime for 2026 and later under HB25-1296, and, in the next sentence, that no addback is required for qualified tips. That is prose, not a table: an addback added or repealed is a sentence somebody has to read, and it changes the state tax of every tipped or hourly filer in Colorado. The bracket figures this shard also carries are the flat rate, which the state adapter handles; this watches the part no parser should touch.

The page where Iowa says, in its own words, that "the starting point for Iowa taxable income is federal taxable income", that it has adopted rolling conformity, and that it will conform with tips, overtime, car loan interest and the senior deduction. Rolling conformity is the thing to watch precisely because it needs no Iowa bill to change what Iowa taxes — the exception list does, and this is the page that carries it.

Idaho conforms STATICALLY, so §63-3004 is a date that moves by bill: today it adopts the Code "as amended and in effect on the first day of January 2026", which is what carries the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's deductions into Idaho. The same section is where a decoupling would be written — it already carves out §85 and the research expensing in §70302 of Pub. L. 119-21. A state whose conformity is a date is the one state where nothing changing federally still changes the answer, and the other way round.

MCA §15-30-2120 is both halves of Montana's answer in one section: subsection (1) starts Montana at federal taxable income, and subsection (2) lists the additions — today §199A and the §164(a)(3) state income tax deduction, neither of which reaches the Act's new deductions. A new subparagraph in (2) is how Montana would take one of them back, and it is a sentence rather than a figure.

N.D.C.C. §57-38-30.3(2) defines North Dakota taxable income as "the federal taxable income ... as computed under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended", adjusted by nine subdivisions — rolling conformity stated inside the rate section itself, which is what makes the federal deductions North Dakota's. The state publishes its Century Code as a chapter PDF, so this watch is chapter-wide and will fire for any amendment anywhere in 57-38, not only this subsection. That is the honest trade: the narrower page does not exist, and a chapter that changes rarely is worth re-reading when it does.

Oregon starts at federal taxable income (ORS 316.048) and takes exactly one of the Act's deductions back: enrolled SB 1507 (2026, ch. 142) §2 adds qualified passenger vehicle loan interest under §163(h)(4) back to federal taxable income for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026. That section is not yet codified in the chapter, which is the reason to watch the chapter rather than a section: the next addback, and this one's codification, both land here. Chapter-wide, so it will fire for unrelated amendments — accepted for the same reason as North Dakota, that the narrow page does not exist.

Every figure on this shard is statutory and none of it indexes yet — §530A(c)(2)(C) starts the inflation adjustment only for taxable years after 2027, so the $5,000 limit is $5,000 in 2026 and in 2027 and there is no annual document for an adapter to chase. Delaware's shape. What the watch is really for here is the part that is not a figure: §530A(a) treats the account as an individual retirement account under §408(a), and (b)(1)(C) sets the two dates the tile turns on — the July 4, 2026 opening and the no-distributions-before-18 rule. Treasury and the IRS are still writing regulations under this section (Notice 2025-68, the March 2026 proposed rules, the August 2026 guidance on eligible investments), which is exactly the condition where a change is a thing a person must read.

The $1,000 pilot contribution and, more importantly, the birth window that decides who gets it: 'born after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2029'. A window with an end date in it is a rule that expires rather than drifts, and when it does the shard should stop offering the money rather than quietly keep adding it to a projection. Second watch on this shard, at the other statute it rests on.
